summary: Provides a framework to help domain managers and zone operators write DNSSEC Policies and DNSSEC Practice Statements. It lists the topics that should be considered, so signers can state clearly how they manage keys and zones. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist for writing down the rules of how you keep a secret stamp safe and use it, so others can decide whether to trust you.

how to write a dnssec policy

subtitle: A checklist of topics for writing a DNSSEC Policy or Practice Statement, so zone operators can show how they manage keys and signing.

tldr.problem: People who depend on a DNSSEC-signed zone, including regulators and other stakeholders, need a consistent way to judge how securely the zone operator manages keys and signing.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines a DNSSEC Policy (what must be done) and a DNSSEC Practice Statement (what is actually done), and gives a common outline of eight components, adapted from the X.509 certificate policy framework of RFC 3647.
tldr.outcome: Policies and Practice Statements written to the same outline can be compared with each other. The framework itself does not define any particular policy or practice.

today: RFC 6841 is an Informational document, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a framework of topics and does not define any particular Policy or Practice Statement.

sections.title: Why DNSSEC Needs Policies and Practice Statements
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses public key cryptography to add data origin authentication, data integrity verification and authenticated denial of existence to the DNS. To let stakeholders judge the strength of the DNSSEC chain of trust, an operator of a signed zone may publish a DNSSEC Practice Statement (DPS) describing its critical security controls and procedures.

The audience is not mainly the relying parties who use signed answers. It is other stakeholders of the DNS infrastructure, which may include regulatory authorities. The document is heavily inspired by RFC 3647 on X.509 certificate policies, though the memo stresses that the DNSSEC trust model is fundamentally different from X.509 PKI.

The framework is a checklist of topics, not a template of answers. It is primarily aimed at Top-Level Domain (TLD) managers and registry operators, though high-value domain holders may use it as a high-level readiness check. Name server and registry system operations are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When many people trust one stamp to prove that mail is real, they want to read how the stamp is kept safe. This memo helps people write that down.

sections.title: Policy Versus Practice Statement
sections.content:
A DNSSEC Policy (DP) sets out the security requirements and standards for a signed zone at a stated level of assurance. It can be the basis for an audit or accreditation, and may apply to several organizations or zones.

A DNSSEC Practice Statement (DPS) describes how one zone operator implements procedures and controls, including how it meets the requirements of any Policy it supports. In the memo's words, the Policy says what needs to be done, and the Practice Statement says what is being done. A DPS is usually more detailed than a Policy and usually applies to a single operator.

Most zone managers do not need a thorough DPS. Publishing one is most relevant for operators of a zone with a significant number of delegations. A DPS should not include sensitive operational details, and it may augment a Policy but generally must not conflict with it, though a Policy authority may allow exceptions where compensating controls give equivalent assurance.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy is the rulebook for the game. The practice statement is a team explaining how it plays by those rules.

sections.title: The Eight-Part Outline
sections.content:
A set of provisions, whether for a DP or a DPS, is organized into eight primary components: Introduction, Publication and Repositories, Operational Requirements, Facility, Management, and Operational Controls, Technical Security Controls, Zone Signing, Compliance Audit, and Legal Matters. Section 5 of the memo gives the full numbered outline.

Drafters may add levels of subcomponents. All components should be present, but a component may be left empty with the words "no stipulation". Having the same structure makes it possible to compare a DPS with a DP to check that it faithfully implements the policy, and to compare two DPSs.

The first two components cover who the document is for and how to reach the responsible organization, plus where the document and public keys are published, whether as trust anchors, in a key hierarchy, or both, and how often new information appears.
sections.plainLanguage: Every report uses the same eight headings, so you can lay two reports side by side and see what is different.

sections.title: Operational and Facility Controls
sections.content:
Operational requirements cover how child zones join the chain of trust: how the child zone manager is identified and later change requests are authenticated, how delegation signer (DS) records are registered and removed, and whether the child must prove possession of the private key matching a DS record.

Facility, management and operational controls describe the non-technical protections. Physical controls include site construction, access, power, water, fire, media storage, waste disposal and off-site backup. Procedural controls name trusted roles and the number of people needed per task (the m of n rule), plus separation of duties. Personnel controls cover qualifications, background checks, training, job rotation, sanctions and contractors.

The same component covers audit logging (what events are recorded and how logs are protected), compromise and disaster recovery, including how keys are rolled over and a new trust anchor is provided, and entity termination, so a transition to another entity is transparent to stakeholders.
sections.plainLanguage: This part asks who can enter the room with the stamp, how many people must be present, how visitors are checked, and what happens if the stamp is stolen.

sections.title: Technical Controls and Zone Signing
sections.content:
Technical security controls protect private keys and activation data such as PINs, passwords or key shares. The questions to answer include who generates key pairs and whether in hardware or software, what standard the cryptographic module meets (the memo gives the US FIPS 140-2 standard as an example), whether the private key is under m of n multi-person control, and whether it is escrowed, backed up or archived. It also asks who may activate, deactivate and destroy the key, and covers computer, network and timestamping controls.

Zone signing covers the key lengths, key types and algorithms and how they can change, the mechanism for authenticated denial of existence (NSEC, NSEC3 or a future mechanism), signature format, key rollover for each key type, RRSIG lifetime and re-signing frequency, verification of records before signing, and time-to-live values for DNSSEC record types. Child zones and relying parties can use this section to understand the signed zone.
sections.plainLanguage: This part asks how the secret stamp is made, where it is locked, who may use it, how often a new one is made, and how long each stamped letter stays good.

sections.title: Audit, Legal Matters and Security
sections.content:
A compliance audit proves compliance with a Policy or a Practice Statement. The document should say how often audits occur, what qualifications the auditor needs, the auditor's relationship to the audited party, which topics are covered, what happens on deficiencies and how results are communicated.

The legal matters component should state the legal status of the binding embodied in DNSSEC signatures and any limits of liability. In most cases a DPS is not a contract, with its terms applied through separate registrar or registrant agreements. At a minimum it should give the jurisdiction in which the registry operates and refer to associated agreements.

The security considerations note that the sensitivity of data protected by DNSSEC varies between tiers of the DNS tree, so each relying party must evaluate its own environment and the chain of trust from its trust anchor to decide how much risk it accepts.
sections.plainLanguage: At the end, an outside checker confirms you really do what you wrote down, and the paper says which country's rules apply if there is an argument.
